stem: Which of the following is untrue about Graves's disease?

options.html: The constellation of signs of this disorder includes pre-tibial myxedema
Pathologic features include scalloping of the thyroid gland and a gland that weighs more than 100g
The antibodies that cause this disorder cause hyperthyroidism by blocking the TSH receptor
RAI uptake and scan will show diffuse iodine uptake within the gland
Patients with this condition can fluctuate between hyper- and hypothyroidism

answer:
The correct answer is C. In Graves disease, thyroid-stimulating antibodies bind the TSH receptor and either stimulate it (causing hyperthyroidism) or, less commonly, block it (causing hypothyroidism) - which is why patients may fluctuate between hyper- and hypothyroid states. Stimulation, not blockade, is the mechanism of the hyperthyroidism, so C is untrue as written.

The TSH-receptor antibodies do not destroy the gland. The entire gland is affected, hence diffuse uptake on RAI scan. Pathologic features include scalloping of the colloid, finger-like projections in the follicles, and an enlarged gland (>100 g).

Hurthle cells are a pathologic finding
This disorder results in destruction of the thyroid gland by T cells

answer: The correct answer is C. Destruction is T cell-mediated, not B cell-mediated. Hashimoto's is a cause of hypothyroidism in which the body produces antibodies against thyroid components - namely TPO or thyroglobulin. Unlike Graves', these antibodies are not stimulatory; instead they signal T cell-mediated destruction of the gland. Pathologic features: lymphoid aggregates, Hurthle cells (follicular cells with increased pink cytoplasm) and fibrosis.

stem: Ms. Smith is a 70 year old female who sustained two fragility fractures including a hip fracture and a wrist fracture. Secondary causes of osteoporosis have been ruled out. Which of the following treatments have been shown to reduce the risk of hip fractures?
answer: The correct answer is E (A, B, D). Raloxifene has not been shown to reduce the risk of hip fractures (it reduces vertebral fracture risk only). risedronate, denosumab and zoledronate all have hip-fracture data. See 06 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Osteoporosis.

stem: Which of the following best describes polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS)?

options.html: A diagnosis of PCOS can be made entirely based on evidence of cystic ovaries on ultrasound.
PCOS can be diagnosed entirely based on history and physical examination.
PCOS is rare compared to other endocrinopathies.
Excess estradiol is a common finding in PCOS.

answer:
The correct answer is B. PCOS is a symptom complex with multiple definitions; a commonly used one requires 2 of 3:

  • Presence of cysts on ovarian imaging
  • Evidence of androgen excess (e.g. acne, hirsutism)
  • Disrupted menstruation (amenorrhea)

Since both androgen excess and disrupted menstruation can be established from history and physical exam alone, B can be correct. A is wrong - cystic ovaries are extremely common and never sufficient alone under any definition. C is wrong - PCOS is common. D is wrong - excess androgens and estrone are found in PCOS; estradiol levels are usually normal.

stem: What statement most accurately describes the hormone abnormalities found in PCOS?

options.html: FSH is constantly overproduced, leading to the development of multiple cystic follicles.
Only androgens produced by the ovaries are found in high concentrations in PCOS; not adrenal sources.
A higher than normal LH surge and LH levels are often found in PCOS.
Most women with PCOS do not yet have any measurable insulin resistance.

answer:
The correct answer is C. In PCOS, LH is relatively overproduced, and LH receptors in thecal and granulosa cells are also overproduced.

A is wrong: FSH is underproduced but at constant levels - the loss of cyclical variation is what forms the cystic follicles. B is wrong: both adrenal and ovarian androgen sources may be overproduced. D is wrong: at least half of women with PCOS already have measurable insulin resistance.

stem: A 32 year old woman presents with complaints of irregular periods over the past 2 years after a long history of regular menses. On physical exam you notice she has some acne present on her face and slightly thinning hair on the top of her head. Her BMI is 29. She tells you she has started having to remove hair on her upper lip frequently. She is "sick of these constant pregnancy scares" and wants something to fix it. You recommend:

options.html: Exercise, diet, and weight loss will be sufficient.

answer:
The correct answer is A. She has two complaints - hirsutism and oligomenorrhea - plus an explicit wish not to conceive. Oral BCPs treat both symptoms and provide the contraception she is asking for, which is why they are the common choice here.

  • Metformin helps oligomenorrhea and may aid fertility - which is not what she wants - and does not address the hirsutism.
  • Clomiphene, a SERM/fertility agent, treats infertility - none of her symptoms.
  • Spironolactone, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, has anti-androgen effects that help hirsutism but not the irregular cycles.
  • E: weight loss may help, but PCOS itself creates a propensity to gain weight, so it may not be sufficient.

stem: Which of the following is not a characteristic of Leydig cells:
answer: The correct answer is B. Leydig cells are located between the seminiferous tubules — it is the Sertoli cells that line the tubule epithelium. Their major function is production of testosterone, via conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone. LH, secreted by the anterior pituitary, stimulates Leydig cells to produce testosterone; testosterone in turn exerts negative feedback on hypothalamic GnRH (the stimulus for both LH and FSH). See 11 - Testicular and Ovarian Function.

stem: Which of the following is a physiological effect of androgens in the male.
answer: The correct answer is B. Androgens are crucial for spermatogenesis and differentiation of the male reproductive tract. Non-reproductive effects: muscle anabolism (so A is the wrong direction), proliferation of chondrocytes and eventual closure of the epiphyseal plate (so D is the wrong direction), and activation of sebaceous glands in the skin. Testosterone exerts a negative effect on LH release from the anterior pituitary and on GnRH from the hypothalamus (so C is the wrong direction).

stem: Which cell of the ovary is the primary producer of estradiol, the major female sex steroid?
answer: The correct answer is B. LH stimulates theca interna cells, which produce androgen for aromatization. Aromatization to estrone occurs in the granulosa cells of the follicle when stimulated by FSH. Both processes are cAMP-mediated. Estrone is immediately converted to estradiol. Both theca interna and granulosa cells are part of the follicle, which becomes the corpus luteum.

stem: What hormone receptor plays a major role in follicular dominance and atresia?
answer: The correct answer is C. Early in the cycle a surge of estrogen causes negative feedback on FSH, so FSH drops. Follicles without enough FSH receptors cannot respond to the lower hormone level and undergo atresia. The dominant follicle expresses more FSH receptors and keeps responding — this follicle then responds to the LH surge and is ovulated. See 10 - Approach to the Menstrual Cycle.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a function of the ovaries?
answer:
The correct answer is D. The ovaries produce estrogen and progesterone — regulating the menstrual cycle, pregnancy and secondary sex characteristics — plus small amounts of testosterone.

FSH is produced by the anterior pituitary, not the ovary. FSH acts on the ovary, stimulating growth and development of the ovarian follicles.

stem: Maureen is a 25-year-old female who presents to your clinic complaining of periods that come anywhere from 20-40 days apart and are very unpredictable. This has been a problem since she started her period at the age of 14 and has become very frustrating. She is also concerned about possible fertility problems. She wants to understand what is happening. In your discussions with her which part of her cycle would you focus on as the most likely culprit?
answer:
The correct answer is A. The follicular (proliferative) phase is dominated by FSH and estrogens and involves growth of the primordial follicle to a tertiary follicle, while the uterine lining grows in preparation for implantation. The follicular phase is usually the cause of cycle-length differences between women — for women with irregular cycles, the follicular phase is often the culprit. Problems in this phase can also cause pregnancy loss and infertility.

The ovulatory phase is preceded by the LH surge and is the release of an oocyte. The luteal (secretory) phase is usually fairly consistent between cycles and between women; it is dominated by LH and progesterone, and implantation can occur during it if fertilization has happened.

stem: Which of the following is matched incorrectly?

options.html: Estrogen causes thickening of the vaginal epithelium
The basalis layer of the uterine endometrium is shed during a menstrual cycle
Abnormal uterine bleeding is an indication for an endometrial biopsy
The endometrial lining becomes receptive to implantation during the secretory phase of the menstrual cycle.

answer: The correct answer is B. It is the functionalis layer of the endometrium that is shed during menses. The basalis layer is retained — it is the regenerative reserve from which the functionalis regrows each cycle.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q30-Q45. Tests [[01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease]].
stem: When is serum cortisol level greatest?

options.html: Cortisol level is unrelated to time

answer:
The correct answer is A. Cortisol release is pulsatile and follows a diurnal rhythm, rising to a maximum at 8 AM then slowly declining through the day. The 8 AM concentration is usually 2-4x the evening concentration.

Why it matters: an 8 AM serum cortisol is useful to test for adrenal insufficiency - if the daily maximum is too low (<100 nmol/L), you can be confident levels are too low all day. That inference cannot safely be made from a PM measurement.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q30-Q45. Tests [[01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease]].
stem: What would be the best test for diagnosing Cushing's syndrome?
answer:
The correct answer is E. With most endocrine disorders the investigative algorithm is the same: first a test to diagnose the disturbance in the axis, then a test to determine etiology (primary vs. secondary vs. tertiary). If the problem is hormone insufficiency, you stimulate; if the problem is overproduction, you suppress.

Cushing syndrome is a syndrome of excessive glucocorticoid activity, so we need a test showing overproduction of cortisol.

  • A (ACTH stimulation) - tests adrenal responsiveness to exogenous ACTH; an etiology test, used to distinguish primary from secondary adrenal insufficiency.
  • B (dexamethasone suppression test) - tests HPA-axis negative feedback; also an etiology test, the hypercortisolism analogue of the ACTH stimulation test. It is the ideal follow-up once Cushing's is diagnosed.
  • C (8 AM serum cortisol) - most useful for adrenal insufficiency, being cortisol at its maximum.
  • D (PM serum cortisol) - can diagnose Cushing's but is a poor test both analytically (single point measurement at a time of fluctuation) and practically (drawing blood in the evening).
  • E (24-hour urinary free cortisol) - best choice: no blood draw, and a 24-hour integrated measure rather than a point value. Diagnostic if >3x the upper limit of normal.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q30-Q45. Tests [[01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease]].
stem:
A 61-year-old female patient was referred to your clinic from the Cardiology outpatient clinic due to hypokalemic hypertension, for which the cardiologist suspected Primary Hyperaldosteronism. Due to budget cuts by the Ontario government, your hospital is underfunded and you can only perform 1 test. Which of the following tests can be used to diagnose Primary Hyperaldosteronism?

i. Aldosterone/Renin Ratio ii. Furosemide Stimulation test iii. 24-hour urine aldosterone iv. Saline Infusion/Fludrocortisone Suppression Test
answer:
The correct answer is D (i and iv). The cardiologist has already established hypokalemia and hypertension; we are testing for etiology, so per the algorithm in Q31 we need a suppression test for aldosterone.

  • Aldosterone/Renin Ratio works because it reflects both the hormone and its stimulatory signal, which is what lets it separate primary from secondary hyperaldosteronism. An elevated ratio means far more aldosterone is produced than the prevailing renin justifies - i.e. aldosterone elevation is independent of its regulatory signal, equivalent to aldosterone staying up after mineralocorticoid or IV salt loading.
  • Saline infusion / fludrocortisone suppression is a good choice for the same reason any suppression test would be.
  • Furosemide stimulation tests responsiveness to stimulatory signals - used for insufficiency, not this.
  • 24-hour urine aldosterone adds nothing: we already know she is hyperaldosteronemic, and urine aldosterone is a poor diagnostic test in isolation.

See primary aldosteronism and 01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease.

stem: Which of the following descriptions is most likely to be a malignant pheochromocytoma?

options.html: Well-circumscribed, 0.5 cm mass in the adrenal cortex with low density of cells of clear adrenal origin with low nuclear pleomorphism
Well-circumscribed, 0.5 cm mass in the adrenal cortex with high cellularity but normal nuclei and normal mitoses
3 well-circumscribed, 0.5 cm masses, all in the adrenal cortex, with capsular invasion but normal nuclei, low cellularity, and normal mitoses
3 well-circumscribed, 0.5 cm masses, 1 in the adrenal cortex, 1 in the liver, and 1 in the thyroid gland, with vascular invasion, high cellularity and mitotic activity, but normal nuclei
1 poorly-circumscribed (i.e. diffuse growth), 1.5 cm mass in the adrenal medulla with profound nuclear pleomorphism, low cellularity, low mitotic rate, and no vascular or capsular invasion.

answer:
The correct answer is D. The point is the criteria for benign vs. malignant pheochromocytoma, formalised as the PASS criteria - which you are unlikely to be expected to memorise for this course.

The one key feature to remember: the only absolute criterion for malignancy is the presence of distant metastases. D is the only option with distant metastases (liver, thyroid). It is also the only mass fulfilling the PASS criteria (score ≥ 4), if confirmation is needed.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q30-Q45. Tests [[01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease]].
stem:
A 51-year-old woman presents to your general endocrine clinic complaining of generalized weakness, fatigue, nausea, and vomiting over the last two months. Also over that time, she reports a weight loss of 30 pounds. Appetite is unchanged from before, but she mentions that she has been adding increasingly large amounts of salt to all food, as she has been craving salt. She is not on any medications. On physical exam, her blood pressure was measured to be 90/60 sitting, in both arms. Upon standing, she became lightheaded and could not maintain balance.

Her blood work shows the following:

MeasurementValueNormal
Hemoglobin (g/L)156120-160
Na (mmol/L)120135-145
K (mmol/L)6.03.5-5.1
8 AM cortisol (nmol/L)200170-635
8 AM ACTH (pmol/L)1402.2-13.3

Based on this information, what is the most likely diagnosis?

options.html: A disease in other organ systems

answer:
The correct answer is B. Lab values are not meaningful without clinical context - do not fixate on the numbers; let them complement the clinical picture.

She is clearly showing signs of adrenal insufficiency. Generalized weakness, fatigue and weight loss are non-specific, but salt craving and orthostatic hypotension point strongly to adrenal insufficiency. From history and physical alone the differential could still include anemia from GI bleeding, and dehydration from malnutrition (given nausea/vomiting).

The bloodwork excludes those and reinforces an endocrine cause:

  • Hemoglobin at the upper end of normal - excludes GI bleeding.
  • Hyperkalemic hyponatremia on no medications - indicates dysregulated mineralocorticoid activity.
  • The 8 AM cortisol is "normal" - but this is not normal at all. In a situation this stressful, where her body cannot even maintain her vitals, cortisol should be much higher.
  • What confirms diagnosis and etiology is the ACTH: 10x the reference range while cortisol sits at the low end of normal. That is a failure to respond to the ACTH signal - equivalent to failing an ACTH stimulation test - so the lesion is at the adrenal: primary adrenal insufficiency.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q30-Q45. Tests [[01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease]].
stem: Which of the following does NOT increase serum cortisol levels?

options.html: Intense or prolonged physical exertion immediately prior to test

answer:
The correct answer is C. Anything affecting either the total amount of cortisol or the amount of cortisol-binding globulin (CBG) can interfere with a serum cortisol measurement.

  • A does interfere - intense or prolonged exertion induces cortisol release.
  • B does - cortisol antagonizes insulin and raises serum glucose, so in hypoglycemia cortisol rises.
  • D and E do - pregnancy and OCP use elevate CBG, and to maintain free cortisol the body synthesizes more, raising the total concentration.
  • C does not: it is unreasonable to release cortisol and raise glucose when glucose is already high.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q30-Q45. Tests [[01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease]].
stem: Which of the following is NOT an action of cortisol?
answer:
The correct answer is D. Cortisol is a stress hormone generating three categories of action:

  1. Increases serum glucose and amino acids
  2. Increases lipid and bone catabolism
  3. Increases mineralocorticoid activity

A and B are mineralocorticoid functions. C is correct - hepatic glucose-liberating activity is upregulated. E is correct - lipid catabolism increases, best illustrated by the skin thinning in Cushing syndrome.

D is the exception: increased peripheral glucose uptake would deplete serum glucose. If a person were hypoglycemic, the body needs what little glucose there is to go to vital organs, not peripheral tissues.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q30-Q45. Tests [[01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease]].
stem: A 48-year-old man has recently been diagnosed with pheochromocytoma and has come to you to be evaluated before surgical resection in one week. He does not take any medications. On physical examination, he appears anxious but otherwise well. BMI is 22. Temperature is 37.0°C, heart rate is 112/min, respiration rate is 16/min, and blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg. Fundoscopic, neurologic, and cardiovascular exams show normal findings. Which of the following would be the next best step in management?

options.html: Hospitalize and give intravenous sodium nitroprusside.

answer:
The correct answer is D. Patients with pheochromocytoma must be pre-treated to stabilize blood pressure before surgery, because both anesthesia and the operation can trigger catecholamine release. The next step is a short-acting alpha-blocker - prazosin, doxazosin or terazosin - targeting a BP of 140/90 to 150/90 mm Hg. Skipping this step can produce a fatal acute hypertensive crisis before or during the operation.

It is critical that beta-blockers are never used before alpha-blockade. Beta-blockade alone leaves unopposed alpha stimulation, giving overwhelming vasoconstriction that can exacerbate or even cause a hypertensive crisis - so C (metoprolol) can be fatal here.

A is wrong for the reason above. B is wrong: even if hydrochlorothiazide lowers BP, it does not address the inappropriate sympathetic activation, and most pheo patients are already vasoconstricted and volume depleted, so a diuretic worsens things. E is wrong: sodium nitroprusside is first-line for acute hypertensive crisis, but this patient is not currently in crisis.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q30-Q45. Tests [[01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease]].
stem: Mutations in which of the following genes is responsible for most (90%) of cases of Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia?
answer:
The correct answer is C. CAH is a disorder of defective adrenal steroid biosynthesis; all genetic causes are autosomal recessive. 21-hydroxylase deficiency accounts for more than 90% of cases - which is why 17-hydroxyprogesterone (the substrate for the 21-hydroxylase reaction) is elevated, and why serum 17-OHP is the standard investigation.

A catalyzes cortisol ↔ cortisone interconversion; does not cause CAH. B can cause CAH but is very rare (and produces an unusual subtype with low androgens and high aldosterone). D converts testosterone → DHT; mutation causes 5-alpha-reductase deficiency, not CAH. E converts testosterone/androstenedione → estrogens; not CAH.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q30-Q45. Tests [[01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease]].
stem: A 3-week-old male infant was found to be homozygous for a mutation in 21-hydroxylase. Which of the following would NOT be expected in his clinical presentation?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Group the features of 21-hydroxylase CAH by hormone abnormality:

  • Substrate buildup: 17-OHP is not consumed, so levels rise → C expected.
  • Cortisol deficiency (precursors need 21-hydroxylase) → hypoglycemia, especially under stress/illness → A expected.
  • Aldosterone deficiency → impaired Na reabsorption, K excretion and H+ excretion → hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis → D and E expected.
  • Androgen excess (excess 17-OHP shunted into androgen synthesis) → in females, virilization (clitoral hypertrophy, labial fusion); in males, inappropriate penile enlargement and scrotal pigmentation.

Because this is a male patient, the expected genital findings are penile enlargement and scrotal pigmentation - not ambiguous genitalia. Hence B is not expected.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q30-Q45. Tests [[01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease]].
stem: Which of the following is INCORRECT regarding pheochromocytomas?
answer:
The correct answer is C. Built around Dr. Bret Wehrli's "Rule of 10s":

  • ~10% arise in association with familial syndromes (MEN2A, MEN2B, VHL, NF1, NF2)
  • ~10% are extra-adrenal
  • ~10% are bilateral
  • ~10% are malignant ← so ~90% are benign, making C the incorrect statement
  • ~10% arise in childhood

The key also walks through reasoning it out if you forget which items the 10% attaches to: tumours are generally rare in children and almost never environmental when they do occur, so "10% childhood" and "10% familial" support each other and are unlikely to be the wrong one. "10% bilateral" is reasonable because it implies 90% unilateral, far more plausible than the inverse - bilateral disease would require either two independent de novo neoplastic events or undetected metastasis to the other gland.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q30-Q45. Tests [[01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease]].
stem: A 41-year-old female presents to your clinic with fatigue, weakness, and lethargy over the last 12 months. She also reports spontaneous, unexplained bruising and weight gain of 40 lbs over the last two months. On physical examination, you notice mild acne, hirsutism, pink striae over the abdomen, moon facies, and a dorsal fat pad. All vital signs were unremarkable. The rest of the physical examination was normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Cushing syndrome is a syndrome of excessive glucocorticoid activity, so look for signs of excess circulating cortisol:

  • Cortisol elevates serum glucose → weight gain from central fat accumulation in a "Cushingoid" distribution (moon facies, dorsal fat pad).
  • Cortisol catabolizes peripheral lipid and protein → skin thinning (digestion of collagen and subcutaneous fat), leaving skin weak and prone to hemorrhage. The likelihood ratio of ecchymoses for Cushing's is 10-11.3. Striae appear from rapid fat expansion plus weakened skin. Muscle weakness develops as muscle is catabolized for amino acids. Osteopenia/osteoporosis follow from osteoblast inhibition plus collagen catabolism.

A (Conn) - no hypokalemic hypertension, so primary aldosteronism does not fit. E - no sympathetic features. D - shares weight gain, fatigue, weakness, lethargy, but the absence of cold intolerance, diminished reflexes, low pulse pressure and bradycardia, plus the presence of steroid-excess signs (acne, hirsutism), makes it unlikely. C - overlaps heavily since hypercortisolism induces insulin resistance, but again the hirsutism and acne favour Cushing's.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q30-Q45. Tests [[01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease]].
stem: In the previous case, what would you order to confirm your diagnosis? Choose one answer.

options.html: Fasting serum glucose and/or HbA1C, followed by 75g Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) if indicated
24 urinary free cortisol, followed by 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (DST) if indicated

answer:
The correct answer is D. This is essentially a matching exercise against Q43's options:

  • A → pheochromocytoma workup
  • B → type 2 diabetes workup
  • C → Conn's syndrome (primary aldosteronism) workup
  • D → Cushing syndrome workup - 24 h urinary free cortisol, then 1 mg overnight DST if indicated
  • E → hypothyroidism workup

lectureMeta: Workbook Q30-Q45. Tests [[01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease]].
stem: A 37-year-old woman presents with a 6 month history of 40 pound weight loss, and a 1 month history of anorexia, recurrent nausea and vomiting, diarrhea, pain, and lightheadedness upon standing. She was diagnosed with Type I diabetes at the age of 9 years; she is currently well-managed with insulin pump therapy. She also was diagnosed with Hashimoto's thyroiditis at age 19; she is currently taking a stable dose of 100 mcg levothyroxine. Family history is significant for hypothyroidism (mother), systemic lupus erythematosus (mother, father), and type I diabetes (brother). Physical examination only reveals orthostatic hypotension and hyperpigmentation of her skin. Which of the following provides the most comprehensive, most likely explanation for her situation?
answer: The correct answer is D. She currently has adrenal insufficiency - orthostatic hypotension plus skin hyperpigmentation (i.e. primary, ACTH-driven) - but in the context of several signs pointing to a global autoimmune condition: she personally has two autoimmune diseases (DM1, Hashimoto's thyroiditis), and her family history is positive for DM1, presumably Hashimoto's, and SLE. The single unifying diagnosis is Polyglandular Autoimmune Syndrome.

stem: What is the name of the outer layer of the cortex and what hormone does it produce?
answer: The correct answer is D. The zona glomerulosa is the outer layer of the cortex and produces aldosterone. None of the other options pairs the correct tissue with the correct hormone. (Mnemonic: GFR - Glomerulosa/Salt, Fasciculata/Sugar, Reticularis/Sex.)

stem:
\* A 59-year old man presents with abdominal pain. A CT scan of the abdomen makes an incidental finding of 1.9 cm left adrenal cortex mass with 20 Hounsfield units. His only past medical history is significant for hypertension and he takes ramipril. What screening tests would you order?

I. 24 hour urine for metanephrines, catecholamines and creatinine II. 1 mg dex suppression test, and ACTH III. Serum aldosterone/renin ratio
answer:
The correct answer is D (all of the above). Because the mass is over 1 cm, any zone of the adrenal gland could be involved. All three investigations are therefore needed to rule in/out:

  • a glucocorticoid issue (Addison's / Cushing's) → 1 mg DST + ACTH
  • a mineralocorticoid issue (hyper/hypoaldosteronism) → aldosterone/renin ratio
  • a catecholamine issue (pheochromocytoma) → 24 h urine metanephrines/catecholamines

lectureMeta: Workbook Q3-Q5. Tests [[02 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Pituitary Gland Disease]].
stem: A male patient with a history of traumatic brain injury presents at your office with anorexia, weight loss, decreased libido, hypoglycemia, constipation, dry skin, low bone mineral density. After ruling out malignancy and reaching a diagnosis, which of the following would not be prescribed?
answer: The correct answer is B. This patient has symptoms of overall hypofunction of the pituitary gland (hypopituitarism), likely secondary to past traumatic brain injury. The key with any hormone deficiency is to replace it, but with a few exceptions. Adrenal insufficiency needs to be replaced with a corticosteroid such as hydrocortisone or prednisone. However, mineralocorticoid replacement is generally only required for primary adrenal insufficiency (such as Addison's disease), and not in this case - in secondary/central disease the aldosterone axis is intact because it is driven by renin-angiotensin, not ACTH. Levothyroxine and testosterone support the thyroid and gonadal axes respectively.

flags.title: Workbook error
flags.html: The key gives the example of mineralocorticoid replacement as "fluticasone". Fluticasone is an inhaled/topical glucocorticoid for asthma and rhinitis, with no mineralocorticoid role at all. The mineralocorticoid used for replacement is fludrocortisone. The letter answer is still B, but for the simpler reason that fluticasone has no place in this patient's regimen.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q3-Q5. Tests [[02 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Pituitary Gland Disease]].
stem: A 40-year-old female was referred to your endocrine office by her family physician. She was recently diagnosed with hypertension. She complains of enlargement of her jaw, nose, and hands. Her heels from 3 years ago no longer fit her and she reports easier flossing. Which one of the following would not be an appropriate finding or primary treatment option for the presenting case?

options.html: Her serum IGF-1 or fasting GH are elevated
A dose of glucose fails to suppress IGF-1
You prescribe her a somatostatin analogue

answer:
The correct answer is D. GH overproduction in an adult is usually the result of a GH-producing adenoma (acromegaly). Patients typically present with increased acral growth (macrognathia, increased space between teeth, enlargement of nose and frontal bones, enlarged hands and feet), hypertrophic arthropathies of joints, hypertension, cardiomyopathy, increased soft tissue (skin thickening, increased polyps, deeper voice, sleep apnea), hypogonadism, and insulin resistance (thus impaired glucose tolerance). Screening findings include increased IGF-1 (produced by the liver under GH), or a failed glucose suppression test (normally glucose should suppress GH to <1 µg/L).

While somatostatin analogues are a possible treatment for GH-producing adenomas, the first-line treatment is transsphenoidal surgery. Hence D is incorrect.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q3-Q5. Tests [[02 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Pituitary Gland Disease]].
stem: A 25-year-old female comes to your office complaining of irregular periods, galactorrhea, headaches and visual disturbances for the past 3 months. You determined that she has a prolactinoma. Which of the following is false?

options.html: She needs to be referred to a surgeon for removal of tumour
Visual disturbances could result from optic chiasm compression by the tumour
Oligomenorrhea is the result of PRL suppressing LH and FSH
Her serum prolactin would unlikely be elevated to > 200 ng/mL

answer: The correct answer is A. Surgery is not first-line treatment for prolactinomas. Dopamine agonists - such as bromocriptine or cabergoline - would be used before considering an operative approach.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q7. Tests [[05 - Disorders of Growth]].
stem: A 6-year-old girl is brought in because her parents are worried due to her slow growth. Records show that she had a normal birth weight and length, and normal growth within the first year of birth. You suspect growth hormone insufficiency. As part of her assessment, you would:

options.html: Perform provocative testing using arginine, clonidine, or glucagon.

answer:
The correct answer is E. The key to this question is that random growth hormone values are NOT useful, due to the pulsatile nature of GH release - hence A and D are incorrect. E is correct because the IGF-1 level is the screening test and provocative testing is diagnostic.

The complete diagnostic criteria for GH deficiency:

  • Short stature - height below 3rd percentile
  • Growth velocity < 25th percentile
  • Bone age delayed by more than 2 SD below chronologic age
  • Inadequate serum GH response to 2 provocative tests (<8 µg/L)

lectureMeta: Workbook Q8-Q12. Tests [[03 - Physiologic Changes that Lead to Puberty]], [[04 - Disorders of Puberty]].
stem: Which of the following is incorrect?

options.html: In girls delayed puberty is defined by no pubertal signs by 13 years of age
Boys are taller than girls because they have an accelerated growth rate during puberty
In early to mid-puberty, LH secretion increased at night
Pulsatile GnRH release is stimulated by Kisspeptin at puberty

answer:
The correct answer is B. B is incorrect - the peak height velocity and total growth during puberty are largely similar between boys and girls. The main reason boys end up taller is that they spend more time growing before the onset of puberty.

A is correct: delayed puberty is defined as the absence or incomplete development of puberty at an age 2.5 SD above the population mean - no pubertal signs by 13 in girls, 14 in boys.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q8-Q12. Tests [[03 - Physiologic Changes that Lead to Puberty]], [[04 - Disorders of Puberty]].
stem: Which of the following is correct?

options.html: Testosterone produced by the Leydig cells promotes Wolffian duct development and Mullerian duct regression
Hypothetically, if a developing male fetus lacked MIS production, they would develop a Mullerian duct instead of a Wolffian duct.
A XY patient with complete androgen insensitivity would be phenotypically female both internally and externally.
Dihydrotestosterone induces the development of external male genitalia

answer:
The correct answer is D. DHT does induce differentiation of the male external genitalia.

A is incorrect - testosterone only stimulates Wolffian duct development; MIS is needed to cause Mullerian duct regression. B is incorrect - without MIS the fetus would develop both a Mullerian and a Wolffian duct, since testosterone production is intact. C is incorrect - an XY patient with CAIS (androgen insensitivity syndrome) has a normal external female phenotype but not a normal internal female phenotype, because SRY is still expressed, MIS is still released from Sertoli cells, and the Mullerian ducts still regress.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q8-Q12. Tests [[03 - Physiologic Changes that Lead to Puberty]], [[04 - Disorders of Puberty]].
stem: Which of the following is incorrect?

options.html: GABA and neuropeptide Y have an inhibitory effect on the hypothalamus GnHR production in females and males respectively
The first sign of puberty in girls is breast enlargement and penile growth in boys
The effect of estrogen during puberty leads to breast tenderness, mood swings, and vaginal discharge
Delayed puberty is defined as a lack of signs of puberty by 13 in girls, and 14 in boys

answer:
The correct answer is B. GABA and NPY are inhibitory and glutamate is stimulatory. Know the Tanner staging of pubic hair, breast and genital development. The order of pubertal staging:

  • Girls: thelarche → growth spurt → pubarche → menarche
  • Boys: testicular enlargement → penile growth → pubarche → growth

So the first sign in boys is testicular enlargement, not penile growth.

Mnemonic from the key: "Estrogen effects are moody, androgen effects are gross."

flags.title: Workbook typo
flags.html: The key writes "glutamine is stimulatory" - it means glutamate. (The stem's own typo, "GnHR", is GnRH.)

lectureMeta: Workbook Q8-Q12. Tests [[03 - Physiologic Changes that Lead to Puberty]], [[04 - Disorders of Puberty]].
stem: A 14-year-old female patient presents in your office. She has breast development and pubic hair but has not started menses. There are no other symptom complaints. She has always been short for her age, although her parents are of reasonable heights. Which of the following is correct?

options.html: Likely constitutional growth delay. Reassure the patient and parents
Order a MRI of head to rule out secondary causes of hypogonadism
Order a karyotype to rule out Turner's syndrome

answer: The correct answer is C. Although constitutional growth delay and secondary hypogonadism are both possible causes of delayed puberty, the most appropriate action is to rule in/out Turner syndrome, which presents with short stature and primary hypogonadism. The patient fits the picture: Turner syndrome patients usually have pubarche, and about 10-15% have breast development as well.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q8-Q12. Tests [[03 - Physiologic Changes that Lead to Puberty]], [[04 - Disorders of Puberty]].
stem: An 8-year-old boy is brought in. He recently developed strong body odour, grew pubic hair and rapid growth in height and weight in the last 6 months. On physical examination his height and weight are at >95% percentiles, bilaterally enlarged testes. Pubic hair T3, penis T5. Which of the following would NOT be consistent or appropriate with this presentation?
answer: The correct answer is B. First determine whether this is a central (gonadotropin-dependent) or peripheral cause of precocious puberty. Because the patient has bilateral testicular enlargement, it is unlikely that the testes are an autonomous source of testosterone - bilateral enlargement means they are being driven by gonadotropins. This is therefore gonadotropin-dependent precocious puberty, so serum LH/FSH would be elevated, not below normal. Treatment is a continuous LHRH analogue, which suppresses pubertal development.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q46-Q47. Tests [[09 - Disorders of Sexual Differentiation]].
stem: What is the expected phenotype of a patient who is 46XY but has a complete defect in the androgen receptor?

options.html: Completely female external and internal genitalia, with normal female puberty and menses
Completely female external and internal genitalia, with no menses but otherwise normal female puberty
Completely female external genitalia, both testes and ovaries, and no menses but otherwise normal puberty
Ambiguous external genitalia, female internal genitalia, and normal female puberty
Completely female external genitalia, only testes internally, and absent menses but otherwise normal female puberty.

answer:
The correct answer is E. This is Complete Androgen Insensitivity.

Internally there will be testes only. Recall that creation of the internal genitalia is sex steroid-independent: testes form under the influence of SRY, and Sertoli cells then generate Mullerian Inhibiting Substance (MIS), which prevents development of the ovaries, fallopian tubes and upper ⅓ of the vagina.

Externally, the lack of androgen signalling at the receptor produces female external genitalia, and at puberty female secondary sex characteristics develop. But because the female internal genitalia are absent, menses does not occur.

See 09 - Disorders of Sexual Differentiation.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q46-Q47. Tests [[09 - Disorders of Sexual Differentiation]].
stem: While conducting a physical examination for an infant with ambiguous external genitalia, you notice a palpable gonad in the inguinal canal. Which of the following is NOT a possibility for the identity of this gonad?
answer: The correct answer is D. The key point, and the whole purpose of palpating for gonads on physical exam: "A PALPABLE GONAD IS NOT AN OVARY." This holds generally even in adults - only extremely thin patients and patients with ovarian pathology have palpable ovaries.

lecture: Development of the female reproductive tract
lectureMeta: Workbook Q1. Taught in the **Endocrinology** block. Tests [[07 - Development of the Female Reproductive System]].
stem: Which of the following structures gives rise to the female external genitalia?
answer: The correct answer is C. Urogenital sinus.

flags.title: No explanation in the workbook
flags.html: The key gives the letter and the phrase only. For context: the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts give the uterus, fallopian tubes and upper vagina; the mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts are the male internal tract and regress in females — note that B and D are the same structure under two names, which is itself a clue.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q6, Q10, Q27, Q45-Q48, Q64, Q136. Taught in the **Endocrinology** block. Tests [[10 - Breast Disorders]], [[11 - Approach to Common Breast Problems]].
stem: In regards to the breast, which of the following is false:

options.html: Benign intraductal papillomas typically present with bloody nipple discharge and are treated by excision
Acute mastitis typically occurs in the setting of lactation
Fibroadenomas are a common benign breast lesion
Fibrocystic change is a pathologic process and fluctuates with the menstrual cycle

answer: The correct answer is D. Fibrocystic change is a physiologic process, not a pathologic one — it does fluctuate with the menstrual cycle. Intraductal papillomas (bloody nipple discharge, excised), acute mastitis (lactational) and fibroadenomas (common, benign) are all correctly described. See 10 - Breast Disorders.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q6, Q10, Q27, Q45-Q48, Q64, Q136. Taught in the **Endocrinology** block. Tests [[10 - Breast Disorders]], [[11 - Approach to Common Breast Problems]].
stem: Which of the following is a concern with tamoxifen, a selective estrogen receptor modulator.
answer: The correct answer is B. Tamoxifen is used in estrogen-dependent breast cancer because it antagonizes estrogen in breast tissue. In endometrial tissue it acts as an agonist (remember estrogen's effects during the menstrual cycle), so an increased risk of endometrial cancer must be considered.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q6, Q10, Q27, Q45-Q48, Q64, Q136. Taught in the **Endocrinology** block. Tests [[10 - Breast Disorders]], [[11 - Approach to Common Breast Problems]].
stem: Fill in the blanks regarding breast tissue development. Estrogen ____________ and progesterone ___________:

options.html: Stimulates fat deposition; stimulates growth of the duct systems
Stimulates growth of the duct systems; promotes lobule development of the mammary glands
Promotes alveoli development of the mammary glands; promotes lobule development of the mammary glands
Promotes lobule development; stimulates fat deposition

answer:
The correct answer is B. estrogen stimulates fat deposition and growth of the duct system of the breast; progesterone promotes development of the lobules and alveoli of the mammary glands.

Note that estrogen does both listed jobs, so A and B each capture half of estrogen's role — B wins because it pairs a true estrogen effect with the correct progesterone effect.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q6, Q10, Q27, Q45-Q48, Q64, Q136. Taught in the **Endocrinology** block. Tests [[10 - Breast Disorders]], [[11 - Approach to Common Breast Problems]].
stem: Which of the following is NOT a concerning feature of a breast mass?
answer: The correct answer is B. A fixed lesion, irregular borders and peau d'orange all suggest a cancerous etiology. Nipple discharge is less concerning because it more often points to a physiologic cause. See 11 - Approach to Common Breast Problems.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q6, Q10, Q27, Q45-Q48, Q64, Q136. Taught in the **Endocrinology** block. Tests [[10 - Breast Disorders]], [[11 - Approach to Common Breast Problems]].
stem: A 27-year-old woman comes in to your clinic with a breast mass that she noticed last month in the shower. She is unsure when exactly it appeared but she thinks it is new. She has no family history of breast cancer. On physical exam the lump feels smooth. What should be your next step in the management of this patient?

options.html: Reexamine her after her next menstrual cycle

answer:
The correct answer is B. In a premenopausal woman with no risk factors, it is appropriate to reassess after the next menstrual cycle — most lumps in this age group are related to menstrual changes.

If she were post-menopausal or high risk, you would investigate immediately, and the modality is age-split: ultrasound under 35, mammogram over 35. Tissue is obtained only if the lump looks concerning on imaging.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q6, Q10, Q27, Q45-Q48, Q64, Q136. Taught in the **Endocrinology** block. Tests [[10 - Breast Disorders]], [[11 - Approach to Common Breast Problems]].
stem: Janet is a 35-year-old woman who comes to your practice inquiring about breast cancer screening. She tells you that she had a maternal grandmother who was diagnosed with breast cancer at 68. She does not know of any other relatives with a history or either breast or ovarian cancer. What should you tell Janet about which investigations (if any) may be appropriate?

options.html: She should start having mammograms every 2-3 years
She should start having mammograms annually
She should go for an ultrasound
She does not currently need to undergo any screening

answer: The correct answer is D. Janet is a regular-risk 35-year-old. She does not meet high-risk criteria for annual screening because she has only a second-degree relative with breast cancer. She has no symptoms of a mass or pain, so an ultrasound is not appropriate either. Janet begins regular screening at age 50.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q6, Q10, Q27, Q45-Q48, Q64, Q136. Taught in the **Endocrinology** block. Tests [[10 - Breast Disorders]], [[11 - Approach to Common Breast Problems]].
stem: Which of the following are common sites of vascular metastasis of breast cancer? Choose all that apply.
answer:
The correct answers are A, B and E. The common sites of vascular metastasis are lungs and pleura, liver, and bone.

F is the distractor worth understanding: breast cancer can extend into the pectoralis muscles, but that is local extension, not vascular metastasis — which is what the question asked. Breast cancer does not commonly spread to the thyroid.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q6, Q10, Q27, Q45-Q48, Q64, Q136. Taught in the **Endocrinology** block. Tests [[10 - Breast Disorders]], [[11 - Approach to Common Breast Problems]].
stem: You see a patient who is concerned about a breast lump. On exam, the lump is fixed in its position, which may mean that the lump has invaded:
answer: The correct answer is D. A breast lump becoming fixed is highly suggestive of invasion into the retromammary space — the space between the pectoralis major muscle and the mammary tissue. Normally the breast moves freely over the chest wall because of the loose connective tissue in that space; tumour invasion adheres the lump to the chest wall, producing the "fixed" finding. None of the other options would explain fixation.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q6, Q10, Q27, Q45-Q48, Q64, Q136. Taught in the **Endocrinology** block. Tests [[10 - Breast Disorders]], [[11 - Approach to Common Breast Problems]].
stem: A 75 year old woman is being followed for an invasive carcinoma of the breast. It is estrogen receptor positive and Her2/neu negative. The patient has previously been diagnosed with osteoporosis. What medical treatment is the best choice?
answer: The workbook's answer is D. Its reasoning: raloxifene is a SERM — full antagonist in breast and endometrium, but partial agonist in bone, so estrogen's protective effects on bone continue, which suits a patient who also has osteoporosis.

flags.title: This answer is clinically wrong — verify before using it
flags.html: Raloxifene is not a treatment for established invasive breast cancer. It is licensed for osteoporosis and for risk reduction in high-risk women. For a 75-year-old with invasive ER+/HER2- disease, endocrine therapy is tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor — and tamoxifen is also a partial agonist in bone in postmenopausal women, so it delivers the very bone benefit the key credits only to raloxifene. On the actual clinical question, B is the better answer; the workbook appears to have swapped the two SERMs' indications.

stem: Which of the following is a correct description of the innervation of the anterior pituitary gland?

options.html: The anterior pituitary (AP) is innervated by parvicellular neurons, which are long neurons that act on the AP via direct innervation.
The anterior pituitary (AP) is innervated by magnocellular neurons, which are long neurons that act on the AP via direct innervation.
The anterior pituitary (AP) is innervated by parvicellular neurons, which are short neurons that act on the AP via the hypophyseal portal system.
The anterior pituitary (AP) is innervated by magnocellular neurons, which are short neurons that act on the AP via the hypophyseal portal system.

answer:
The correct answer is C. Although this looks very specific, the key notes something similar has been asked on past exams. The anterior pituitary is served by short parvocellular neurons, which release hormones into the hypophyseal portal system, which in turn stimulates the AP.

Contrast the posterior pituitary, which is directly innervated by longer magnocellular neurons. Mnemonic: magnocellular neurons are longer, so they can reach the posterior pituitary directly.

stem: Which one of the following is correct?

options.html: Compression of the optic chiasm by a pituitary tumour can lead to a loss of vision in one eye.
In a patient presenting with a suspected pituitary tumour compressing the optic chiasm a classic finding when assessing visual fields is bitemporal hemianopsia or bitemporal superior quadrantanopia.
Because the anterior pituitary has a portal venous vascular supply, it is more prone to ischemia, resulting in Sheehan's Syndrome.

answer: The correct answer is D. A is incorrect - a pituitary tumour compressing the optic chiasm produces bitemporal hemianopsia, because the fibres crossing at the chiasm are those carrying the left field of view from the left eye and the right field of view from the right eye. Compressing them knocks out the temporal fields of both eyes. B and C are both correct.

lecture: CBL Case 1 - Hyperglycemia Refractory to Insulin
lectureMeta: 46-year-old woman, longitudinal case adapted from NEJM Case 10-2024. See [[13 - Antihyperglycemic Drug Choices for T2DM (CBL)]].
stem: A 46-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is maintained on insulin glargine 30 units daily, insulin lispro 10 units three times daily with meals, and glimepiride. Her fasting glucose has been running 5.5-7.0 mmol/L but her 2-hour post-prandial readings are consistently 15-18 mmol/L, and her A1C is 11.0%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next change to her regimen?

options.html: Increase insulin glargine to 40 units daily
Increase the pre-meal insulin lispro dose
Replace insulin glargine with NPH insulin twice daily
Add a bedtime dose of insulin lispro

answer:
B. The decision here is which defect is uncontrolled, not how much insulin to give. Her fasting glucose is at target, so the basal component is doing its job - escalating glargine (A) would push her toward overnight hypoglycemia without touching the problem. The abnormality is confined to the post-prandial window, which is the prandial insulin's territory.

  • C swaps one basal for another; NPH's peak would add hypoglycemia risk, not prandial coverage.
  • D stimulates insulin secretion in a glucose-independent way and would compound the hypoglycemia risk she already carries on a secretagogue plus insulin.
  • E puts rapid-acting insulin where there is no meal, which is how nocturnal hypoglycemia is caused.

Principle: match the agent's time-action profile to the interval that is out of range. Fasting out of range → basal; post-prandial out of range → prandial.

lecture: CBL Case 1 - Hyperglycemia Refractory to Insulin
lectureMeta: 46-year-old woman, longitudinal case adapted from NEJM Case 10-2024. See [[13 - Antihyperglycemic Drug Choices for T2DM (CBL)]].
stem: The same patient is now taking glimepiride, pioglitazone, insulin glargine and insulin lispro. Which adverse effect should you counsel her about as the most likely consequence of this particular combination?
answer:
B. Three agents that lower glucose by three different routes are stacked - a secretagogue, a sensitizer, and exogenous insulin - so the additive hypoglycemia risk is the immediate safety issue. Separately, all three of SUs, TZDs and insulin drive weight gain, and pioglitazone adds fluid retention on top.

  • A belongs to metformin, which she is no longer taking.
  • C belongs to the SGLT2 inhibitors - relevant to her earlier empagliflozin, not this regimen.
  • D belongs to the AGIs.
  • E is a concern for the incretin-based agents, none of which she is on.

Principle: when a regimen stacks agents, ask what the shared toxicity is. Here two mechanisms converge on hypoglycemia and three converge on weight.

lecture: CBL Case 1 - Hyperglycemia Refractory to Insulin
lectureMeta: 46-year-old woman, longitudinal case adapted from NEJM Case 10-2024. See [[13 - Antihyperglycemic Drug Choices for T2DM (CBL)]].
stem: Two years earlier, empagliflozin had been added to her regimen. Two months later she presented with dysuria and urinary frequency; urine culture grew E. coli. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.html: Treat the infection, counsel on hygiene and fluid intake, and continue empagliflozin
Discontinue empagliflozin permanently and treat the infection
Treat the infection and add prophylactic daily antibiotics
Discontinue empagliflozin and substitute an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor
Withhold antibiotics and increase fluid intake alone

answer:
A. A single uncomplicated urinary tract infection is an expected, mechanism-predictable event on an SGLT2 inhibitor - glucose delivered into the urinary tract is a bacterial substrate - and it is not by itself a reason to abandon a drug that is working. Treat the infection and keep the agent, with counselling.

  • B is the right call only for recurrent or severe genitourinary infection, or urosepsis. Discarding the class after one event costs her the glycemic, weight and cardiorenal benefit.
  • C commits her to antibiotic exposure and resistance risk after a first uncomplicated episode.
  • D substitutes a weaker agent and does not follow from a UTI.
  • E undertreats a culture-positive infection in a patient with diabetes.

Principle: distinguish an anticipated, manageable adverse effect from one that mandates stopping the drug. Frequency and severity decide, not the first occurrence.

stem: Six months before presentation she was admitted with abdominal pain; endoscopy showed erosive gastritis and duodenitis due to H. pylori, and she was started on amoxicillin, clarithromycin, bismuth subsalicylate and pantoprazole. She remains on glimepiride, pioglitazone and insulin. Two days later she has repeated morning capillary glucose readings of 2.8-3.3 mmol/L. Which of the following best explains this?

options.html: Amoxicillin displaces glimepiride from plasma protein binding sites
Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4, raising glimepiride and pioglitazone levels
Pantoprazole reduces the subcutaneous absorption of insulin glargine
Bismuth subsalicylate increases the renal clearance of insulin
Eradication of H. pylori abruptly increases insulin sensitivity

answer:
B. This is the pharmacokinetic trap in the case. Clarithromycin is a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor; both glimepiride (a sulfonylurea) and pioglitazone undergo extensive hepatic metabolism, so inhibiting their clearance raises drug levels and converts a stable regimen into a hypoglycemic one. Bismuth subsalicylate may contribute a hypoglycemic effect of its own, which the lecture noted alongside the interaction.

  • A - protein-binding displacement is the reflex exam answer, but it is the wrong mechanism for amoxicillin here.
  • C - acid suppression is irrelevant to a parenteral drug.
  • D - insulin is not renally cleared in a way bismuth alters.
  • E - plausible-sounding, but far too slow and too small to produce hypoglycemia within 48 hours.

Principle: whenever glycemic control changes abruptly and the diabetes regimen did not, look at what was added for something else.

lecture: CBL Case 1 - Hyperglycemia Refractory to Insulin
lectureMeta: 46-year-old woman, longitudinal case adapted from NEJM Case 10-2024. See [[13 - Antihyperglycemic Drug Choices for T2DM (CBL)]].
stem: Over the following 21 months her BMI falls from 45.6 to 17.0 (weight 42 kg) despite escalating insulin. She is cachectic with diffuse loss of fat and muscle, and has developed acromegaly-like facial features, extensive acanthosis nigricans, skin tags and vitiligo. Her A1C remains 11.0-14.0% and her total insulin requirement now exceeds 50 units/kg/day. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?

options.html: Covert non-adherence to her insulin regimen
Autoantibodies directed against the insulin receptor

answer:
C. Type B insulin resistance. Three features converge: an insulin requirement an order of magnitude above ordinary resistance (>50 units/kg/day against a typical 0.5-1), severe acanthosis nigricans and skin tags as the cutaneous signature of extreme insulin-receptor signalling failure, and vitiligo marking a broader autoimmune diathesis. The catabolic wasting despite massive insulin doses is the giveaway that insulin is being delivered but not acting.

  • A cannot explain hyperglycemia that persisted through supervised inpatient IV insulin infusions across six admissions.
  • B - acromegaly causes insulin resistance and coarse features, but not vitiligo, and not resistance of this magnitude.
  • D is congenital; she had a BMI of 45.6 five years earlier, so a lifelong lipodystrophy is excluded by her own history.
  • E would give central obesity with proximal myopathy, not diffuse cachexia.

Principle: insulin resistance severe enough to defeat IV insulin is a receptor or post-receptor problem, not a dosing problem. The skin is where you read it.

lecture: CBL Case 1 - Hyperglycemia Refractory to Insulin
lectureMeta: 46-year-old woman, longitudinal case adapted from NEJM Case 10-2024. See [[13 - Antihyperglycemic Drug Choices for T2DM (CBL)]].
stem: Which single investigation would best confirm the diagnosis in the patient above?
answer:
C. The target of the autoantibody is the diagnosis, so the assay must be directed at the receptor.

  • B is the trap. Anti-insulin antibodies and anti-insulin receptor antibodies are different tests answering different questions. The former bind the hormone and are largely a consequence of exogenous insulin exposure; only the latter establish type B insulin resistance.
  • A would test for acromegaly - reasonable to send given the facial features, but it explains neither the vitiligo nor receptor-level resistance.
  • D tests β-cell autoimmunity, which speaks to type 1 diabetes and does not cause resistance of this magnitude.
  • E screens for hypercortisolism, already argued against by the body habitus.

Principle: when the mechanism is antibody-mediated, name the antigen before you order the test.

stem:
A 47-year-old man with type 2 diabetes diagnosed 2 years ago takes metformin BID and presents with fatigue and headache. He works as a consultant engineer, travels several days most weeks, struggles to maintain diet and exercise, and often forgets his second daily dose. He has gained 12 lb in the past year. He has a history of IBS.

ParameterResultFlag
fasting glucose178 mg/dLhigh
creatinine1.0 mg/dL
A1C8.3%high
total cholesterol250 mg/dLhigh
LDL150 mg/dLhigh
triglycerides220 mg/dLhigh

Which of the following is the most appropriate second agent?

options.html: Repaglinide three times daily with meals

answer:
C. Every one of his problems points the same way. Weight gain of 12 lb and dyslipidemia call for an agent that produces weight loss; his normal creatinine leaves the class available; and the decisive practical factor is that he already fails a twice-daily schedule, so a once-weekly injection is the dosing interval most likely to actually be taken.

  • A and B both cause weight gain in a patient whose weight is already the problem, and the SU adds hypoglycemia risk to an irregular travelling schedule.
  • D requires dosing with every meal - the worst fit for his adherence - and his IBS rules it out on tolerability grounds anyway (Q8).
  • E is three times daily, is a secretagogue with hypoglycemia risk, and causes weight gain.

Principle: when efficacy is comparable across several classes, the tie is broken by weight, hypoglycemia risk, and a dosing frequency the patient will keep to.

lectureMeta: 47-year-old man on metformin monotherapy. See [[13 - Antihyperglycemic Drug Choices for T2DM (CBL)]].
stem: For the same patient, which drug class is contraindicated by his medical history?
answer:
C. The lecture's caution-and-contraindication table lists chronic intestinal disorders and obstruction as contraindications to the AGIs - and his IBS is exactly that. The mechanism makes it obvious: undigested carbohydrate delivered to the colon and fermented there produces flatulence, bloating and cramping, which is to say it reproduces and worsens his existing symptoms.

  • A, B and D carry cautions in renal and hepatic dysfunction, which he does not have (creatinine 1.0).
  • E he already takes uneventfully.

Principle: an adverse-effect profile that overlaps a patient's existing symptoms is a contraindication, not merely a caution.

lectureMeta: 47-year-old man on metformin monotherapy. See [[13 - Antihyperglycemic Drug Choices for T2DM (CBL)]].
stem: Before starting a GLP-1 receptor agonist in this patient, which element of the history would most strongly contraindicate it?

options.html: A family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma

answer:
B. Medullary thyroid carcinoma and multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type 2 are listed contraindications to the GLP-1 and GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists, so a family history is the item here that stops the prescription.

  • A and C are cautions worth noting - gallbladder disease, and delayed gastric emptying or gastroparesis, appear in the caution column - but neither is an absolute bar.
  • D and E are indications to prefer the class, not reasons to avoid it.

Principle: read a drug table in two columns. Caution changes your monitoring; contraindication changes your choice.

lecture: CBL Case 3 - Nancy (Secondary Failure and Hypoglycemia Fear)
lectureMeta: 62-year-old woman on maximum-dose dual oral therapy. See [[13 - Antihyperglycemic Drug Choices for T2DM (CBL)]].
stem: A 62-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes of 5 years takes maximum-dose metformin; gliclazide was added last year, which brought her A1C from 7.8% to 7.1%. Today her A1C is 7.9% on maximum doses of both, and she has gained 5 lb since starting gliclazide (BMI 26). She reports taking both medications reliably. Which of the following best explains her loss of glycemic control?

options.html: Progressive β-cell failure with secondary sulfonylurea failure
A drug interaction reducing gliclazide absorption

answer:
A. The pattern is diagnostic: a real but temporary response to a secretagogue (7.8% → 7.1%), followed by drift back up on an unchanged maximum dose. A sulfonylurea works only through β-cells that can still secrete; as β-cell mass and function decline, and as the K⁺/ATP channel target desensitizes, the drug runs out of substrate to act on.

The follow-on the case asks: would glyburide or repaglinide have been better? No - both act on the same K⁺/ATP channel in the same failing β-cell. Switching within the secretagogue mechanism cannot recover a mechanism that is exhausted. She needs a class that does not depend on β-cell secretory reserve.

  • B is not a recognised phenomenon at this target.
  • C would bring weight loss, ketosis-prone decompensation and a far steeper deterioration, not a 0.8% drift.
  • D is contradicted by the history, and would not have produced the initial clean response.
  • E would be an abrupt change traceable to a new medication; she takes none.

Principle: initial response then progressive failure on an unchanged dose is the signature of secondary failure, and it tells you to change mechanism, not dose.

lecture: CBL Case 3 - Nancy (Secondary Failure and Hypoglycemia Fear)
lectureMeta: 62-year-old woman on maximum-dose dual oral therapy. See [[13 - Antihyperglycemic Drug Choices for T2DM (CBL)]].
stem: The same patient's stated goals are to control her glycemia, lose weight, avoid hypoglycemia, and stay on affordable oral therapy. She refuses insulin because she dislikes needles and fears hypoglycemia, since her eating is inconsistent. She is unemployed and cares for her mother, who has dementia. Which of the following is the most appropriate addition?
answer:
B. It is the only option that satisfies the constraints she has actually set: oral, weight loss rather than gain, low intrinsic hypoglycemia risk because its action is insulin-independent, and cardiorenal benefit as a bonus. Crucially it does not depend on the β-cell reserve that has already failed her (Q10).

The honest tension: cost. She is unemployed and paying out of pocket, and an SGLT2 inhibitor is not cheap - so coverage has to be checked, and it is the one goal this choice may not meet. A DPP-4 inhibitor is the reasonable alternative if cost is prohibitive: oral, very low hypoglycemia risk, but weight neutral rather than weight-reducing, and more modest efficacy.

  • A stays inside the mechanism that is failing, and picks the worst SU for hypoglycemia (Q12).
  • C gives weight gain, fracture risk in a 62-year-old woman, and higher cost - three of her four goals violated.
  • D is explicitly refused, and her irregular eating makes her fear of hypoglycemia legitimate rather than irrational.
  • E requires dosing with every meal in someone who eats inconsistently, and is again a secretagogue.

Principle: patient-stated goals are selection criteria. Score each candidate class against all of them and the answer usually declares itself.

lecture: CBL Case 3 - Nancy (Secondary Failure and Hypoglycemia Fear)
lectureMeta: 62-year-old woman on maximum-dose dual oral therapy. See [[13 - Antihyperglycemic Drug Choices for T2DM (CBL)]].
stem: Given her inconsistent eating pattern and her role as sole caregiver, which agent would carry the greatest risk of hypoglycemia for this patient?
answer:
A. Among the sulfonylureas, glyburide carries the highest hypoglycemia risk - longest effective duration of action, active metabolites, and the least forgiving profile when a meal is missed. It is also the SU avoided earliest as renal function declines. In a patient who eats irregularly and is responsible for someone with dementia, a prolonged unrecognised hypoglycemic episode is the specific harm to avoid.

  • B is a sulfonylurea and carries real risk, but less than glyburide - which is why gliclazide, glimepiride and repaglinide tolerate moderate impairment better.
  • C acts in a nutrient-dependent way, so it does not drive insulin secretion in the absence of a meal.
  • D and E carry no hypoglycemia risk as monotherapy; neither increases insulin secretion.

Principle: hypoglycemia risk tracks with glucose-independent insulin secretion and with duration of action. Ask what the drug does when the patient skips a meal.

lecture: CBL Case 4 - Albert (SGLT2 Inhibitor, AKI and Shock)
lectureMeta: 72-year-old man admitted to ICU. See [[13 - Antihyperglycemic Drug Choices for T2DM (CBL)]].
stem: A 72-year-old man is admitted to the ICU with acute kidney injury and severe shock. For 3 days he has felt unwell with foot swelling, decreased urine output, nausea and shortness of breath. He has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and GERD. Medications: valsartan, hydrochlorothiazide, canagliflozin, sitagliptin, metformin, insulin degludec, insulin aspart and pantoprazole. His capillary glucose is 9.1 mmol/L. Which investigation is most important to obtain now?
answer:
A. He is acutely unwell on an SGLT2 inhibitor, which puts euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis at the top of the list - and the glucose of 9.1 mmol/L is precisely why it gets missed. Urinary glucose loss blunts the hyperglycemia you would ordinarily use as the trigger to test for DKA, so a near-normal glucose does not exclude it. Measure ketones regardless of the glucose reading.

A serum lactate is the strong second call: he is on metformin with an acute drop in renal clearance and tissue hypoperfusion from shock, which is the exact setting for lactic acidosis.

  • B describes the last three months and changes nothing today.
  • C has no role in established type 2 diabetes in an emergency.
  • D does not explain this presentation.
  • E is reasonable in a shock workup, but it is not the test uniquely likely to be overlooked here.

Principle: when a drug removes the sign you normally screen on, screen on something else. Ketones in any unwell patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor.

lecture: CBL Case 4 - Albert (SGLT2 Inhibitor, AKI and Shock)
lectureMeta: 72-year-old man admitted to ICU. See [[13 - Antihyperglycemic Drug Choices for T2DM (CBL)]].
stem: Which of the following best explains the mechanism of this patient's AKI and shock?

options.html: Osmotic diuresis from canagliflozin compounded by hydrochlorothiazide and valsartan, causing volume depletion and prerenal AKI
Metformin accumulation causing lactic acidosis as the primary event
Excess insulin degludec causing hypoglycemic collapse

answer:
A. Three drugs pull in the same direction on his intravascular volume: canagliflozin produces glucosuria and osmotic diuresis, hydrochlorothiazide adds natriuretic volume loss, and valsartan removes the angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar tone that would otherwise defend glomerular filtration pressure as volume falls. Layer an acute illness with poor intake on top and you get severe dehydration, hypotension, reduced renal perfusion and prerenal AKI.

  • B inverts cause and effect. Metformin-associated lactic acidosis is a consequence of the AKI and hypoperfusion here, not the initiating event - though it is a reason to hold metformin now.
  • C and E are genuine drug causes of AKI, but neither fits: no eosinophilia, rash or fever is described, no new drug was started, and neither explains shock.
  • D is excluded by the glucose of 9.1 mmol/L.

Principle: in polypharmacy, look for drugs whose effects converge on one physiological axis. Three volume-depleting agents is not three small risks; it is one large one.

lecture: CBL Case 4 - Albert (SGLT2 Inhibitor, AKI and Shock)
lectureMeta: 72-year-old man admitted to ICU. See [[13 - Antihyperglycemic Drug Choices for T2DM (CBL)]].
stem: Reviewing his records, which feature of the preceding 18 months should have prompted reassessment of his regimen?

options.html: Recurrent falls attributed to postural hypotension
The foot swelling of the last 3 days

answer:
A. canagliflozin was started roughly 18 months earlier, and over that same period he had several falls due to postural hypotension. That is the clinical readout of established volume depletion, and it was a standing invitation to review an SGLT2 inhibitor plus a thiazide plus an ARB in a 72-year-old. The ICU admission was the endpoint of a process that had been signalling for a year and a half.

  • B is reassuring on glycemia and says nothing about volume status - which is the trap: his diabetes looked well managed.
  • C is unrelated.
  • D is the absence of a trigger for review, not a warning sign.
  • E is part of the acute presentation, not the preceding window the question asks about.

Principle: postural symptoms and falls in an older patient on volume-depleting drugs are a medication review trigger, not an incidental geriatric finding.

lecture: CBL Case 4 - Albert (SGLT2 Inhibitor, AKI and Shock)
lectureMeta: 72-year-old man admitted to ICU. See [[13 - Antihyperglycemic Drug Choices for T2DM (CBL)]].
stem: He recovers with fluid resuscitation. At discharge his eGFR has stabilised at approximately 28 mL/min. Which of the following best describes the correct approach to his canagliflozin?

options.html: Restart at full dose immediately for glycemic control
It is permanently contraindicated at this eGFR and must be stopped for good
It should not be newly initiated at this eGFR, but may be continued once he is euvolemic, for cardiorenal benefit

answer:
C. The SGLT2 inhibitors sit in a "do not initiate, but may continue" band below an eGFR threshold, and the reason is the key idea from this session: cardiorenal benefit is preserved even where glucose-lowering efficacy falls off. The drug stops being much of a glucose-lowering agent at this eGFR while remaining worth taking for the kidney and the heart. What must be fixed is the volume context - restart only once he is euvolemic, and revisit the thiazide and the ARB alongside it.

  • A ignores the volume depletion that put him in the ICU.
  • B overcorrects and discards the cardiorenal indication.
  • D picks the sulfonylurea most likely to cause hypoglycemia and the one avoided earliest in renal impairment - the wrong drug for a 72-year-old with an eGFR of 28.
  • E goes the wrong way: metformin requires stepwise reduction as eGFR falls, not maximisation.

Principle: an agent's indication can outlive its original purpose. Ask what you are now prescribing it for.

stem: A 68-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes has an eGFR of 12 mL/min. His A1C is 8.4% and his oral agents are being reviewed. Which of the following glucose-lowering options can still be prescribed?
answer:
The correct answer is D, insulin. Graded in-class poll key: 14 of 15 responses chose insulin, marked "Is correct".

Insulin has no renal cut-off - it is titrated to effect, which is exactly what lets it survive to the lowest eGFR. Everything else here is limited by renal clearance:

  • A requires stepwise dose reduction as eGFR falls and is then avoided outright at the lowest ranges; an eGFR of 12 is well past that.
  • B is renally cleared and needs dose reduction. Note the discriminator: linagliptin is the DPP-4 inhibitor requiring no adjustment, because its clearance is non-renal.
  • C accumulates, and the resulting hypoglycemia is prolonged and dangerous.

Principle: at the extremes of renal function, ask which agent's dose is set by titration rather than by clearance.

stem: An 84-year-old woman lives alone with mild cognitive impairment. Her eGFR is 45 mL/min and her A1C is 8.0% on metformin alone. Avoiding hypoglycemia is the dominant priority. Which drug class is among the safest options for her?
answer:
The correct answer is A, the DPP-4 inhibitors. Graded in-class poll key: 15 of 16 responses chose DPP-4 inhibitors, marked "Is correct".

They are well tolerated, weight neutral, and carry minimal hypoglycemia risk because they act in a nutrient-dependent way - amplifying incretin-driven insulin secretion only when a meal has been eaten. That is the property that protects a frail patient living alone who may skip meals. Linagliptin needs no renal dose adjustment.

  • B brings volume depletion, postural hypotension and fall risk in exactly this demographic - see Q13-16.
  • C is the worst choice here: glucose-independent secretion, plus prolonged action, plus living alone, plus cognitive impairment is the recipe for unrecognised severe hypoglycemia.
  • D brings fluid retention, HF risk and fracture risk in an 84-year-old.

Principle: in the frail elderly the target shifts from tight control to avoiding harm; pick the class whose mechanism is self-limiting.

stem: Molly Flanders is a 26-year-old woman with 5 cycles in the past year, acne and excess facial hair. She has had no period for 4 months, and in the last two months has been up at least once a night with nocturia and has had three yeast infections. She and her partner would like to have a baby. Exam: height 1.50 m, weight 81 kg (BMI ~36 kg/m²), BP 135/85, mild facial hirsutism, acanthosis and skin tags on the neck, no Cushingoid stigmata. Labs: A1c 6.7%, fasting plasma glucose 7.4 mmol/L. Which pair of diagnoses best fits this presentation? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Impaired glucose tolerance and a prolactinoma

answer:
The correct answer is B, type 2 diabetes and PCOS/PMOS.

Why T2D fits: she is symptomatic (polydipsia, nocturia) with a fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L and an A1c ≥6.5% - either one is diagnostic in a symptomatic patient. BMI ~36 kg/m², acanthosis and skin tags all point to insulin resistance. The absence of wide purple striae, proximal muscle weakness, thin skin over the dorsum of the hand and spontaneous bruising argues against Cushing's and so against secondary diabetes. PCOS/PMOS is itself a T2DM risk factor. T1DM is not completely impossible.

Why PCOS/PMOS fits: she meets the Rotterdam criteria - clinical hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne) plus ovulatory dysfunction (oligomenorrhea) - which is 2 of 3 after exclusions.

stem: Molly is symptomatic. According to the Diabetes Canada criteria used in this session, how many abnormal tests are required to diagnose diabetes in a symptomatic patient, and how many in an asymptomatic one? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: One abnormal test if symptomatic; two abnormal tests on different days if asymptomatic
Two abnormal tests if symptomatic; one abnormal test if asymptomatic
Two abnormal tests on different days in both cases
One abnormal test in both cases, provided it is an A1c

answer:
The correct answer is A. Diabetes Canada 2018: a symptomatic patient (polydipsia, polyuria/nocturia, weight loss) needs ONE of - fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L, A1c ≥6.5%, 2-hour OGTT ≥11.1 mmol/L, or random plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L. An asymptomatic patient needs TWO abnormal tests on different days.

The OGTT is rarely used now outside GDM screening, and should be avoided where there is already symptomatic hyperglycemia.
