stem: Which set of criteria defines PCOS, and what did the 2023 update change? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Rotterdam criteria - 2 of 3; the 2023 update allows AMH to replace ultrasound in defining polycystic ovarian morphology
Rotterdam criteria - all 3 required; the 2023 update added fasting insulin as a fourth criterion
NIH criteria - hyperandrogenism alone; the 2023 update added obesity as a requirement
Rotterdam criteria - 2 of 3; the 2023 update removed hyperandrogenism from the criteria

answer:
The correct answer is A. The Rotterdam criteria require 2 of 3, after exclusions:

  • clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism
  • ovulatory dysfunction (e.g. irregular cycles)
  • polycystic ovarian morphology (PCOM) on ultrasound

2023 update: AMH may replace ultrasound to define PCOM. AMH reflects the antral follicle count, so it reduces the need for transvaginal ultrasound. Use it only where it is needed to complete the criteria.

stem: Molly and her partner are trying to conceive. Which single test is the most important to obtain before deciding on her management? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: A transvaginal ultrasound for ovarian morphology

answer:
The correct answer is B, a serum beta-hCG - she could be pregnant, and the entire management plan forks on the result.

The rest of the workup in a newly diagnosed patient with T2DM who is contemplating pregnancy: serum creatinine and urine ACR, lipids, an optometry exam to screen for diabetic eye disease, and a foot exam including monofilament to screen for peripheral sensory neuropathy. A CBC is reasonable to confirm the A1c is reliable. For PCOS/PMOS, a total testosterone level.

  • A should be avoided where there is already symptomatic hyperglycemia.
  • D is not indicated - she has no Cushingoid stigmata.

stem: Molly's pregnancy test is negative. Which management plan best fits the facilitator's approach? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Start insulin, target A1c <5.0%, and recheck in one month
Refer to the Diabetes Education Centre, low threshold for metformin, pre-conception A1c target <6.5%, recheck A1c in 3-4 months
Start a sulfonylurea and begin home glucose monitoring immediately
Lifestyle change alone, with no drug therapy until the A1c exceeds 8.0%

answer:
The correct answer is B. Refer to the DEC for education, diet and activity, with a long-term weight-control goal. Have a low threshold for metformin - it is the safest oral agent in pregnancy and it also helps induce ovulation in PCOS, which matters because she is trying to conceive. The pre-conception A1c target is <6.5%. Recheck the A1c in 3-4 months.

Home glucose monitoring only if starting a drug that can cause hypoglycemia - which metformin does not.

stem: Steve Dedalus is 37 and has had type 1 diabetes for 27 years. His most recent A1c is 11.0%. What does the A1c measure, and over what period? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Glucose irreversibly attached to hemoglobin, reflecting ambient plasma glucose over the preceding ~90 days
Fasting glucose averaged over the preceding 7 days
Total glycated serum protein over the preceding ~14 days
Peak post-prandial glucose over the preceding ~30 days

answer:
The correct answer is A. The A1c measures glucose irreversibly attached to hemoglobin (glycosylation), and reflects ambient plasma glucose over the preceding ~90 days in a patient with normal hemoglobin dynamics.

It is the best-validated measure of long-term structural-complication risk: clinical trials show clinically important reductions in the onset and progression of diabetic eye disease, neuropathy and nephropathy when the A1c is lowered.

stem: Steve's A1c is 11.0%. Roughly half of patients with type 1 diabetes of 10 years or more will not reach an A1c below 7.0%. Which statement best captures his glycemic goal of care? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Target A1c ≤7.0% without unacceptable hypoglycemia; and because risk falls continuously with A1c, any improvement still lowers complication risk
Target A1c ≤7.0%; if it cannot be reached, there is no benefit to partial improvement
Target A1c <6.0%, accepting frequent hypoglycemia as the cost of control
No target is appropriate in longstanding type 1 diabetes

answer:
The correct answer is A. The target is A1c ≤7.0% without unacceptable hypoglycemia, and "unacceptable" is patient-specific - for example severe (assist-requiring) lows, or frequent (daily) self-treated lows.

The key point: at least half of patients with T1D for ≥10 years will not reach an A1c <7.0%, but because risk falls continuously with A1c, any improvement still lowers complication risk - going from 11.0% to 9.5% is worth having even though it misses the target.

To reach ≤7.0%: fasting / ac-meal glucose ~4.0-7.0 mmol/L, and 2-hour post-prandial ~5.0-10.0 mmol/L.

stem: Steve's fingerstick values over two weeks range from 2 to 20 mmol/L. Before escalating his regimen, which step does the facilitator put first? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Immediately switch him to an insulin pump
Identify the sources of glycemic variability - injection sites, insulin timing, over-correction of lows, and his bolus-dosing system
Add a sulfonylurea to his insulin

answer:
The correct answer is B. A range of 2 to 20 mmol/L is a variability problem, and you cannot fix variability by adding insulin. Look first for:

  • injection-site problems - is there lipohypertrophy?
  • timing of the NovoRapid relative to meals (~15 minutes before)
  • over-correcting lows
  • whether he has a system for pre-meal bolus dosing based on the glucose level plus expected carbohydrate intake
  • possible gastroparesis

Then offer referral to the Diabetes Education Centre, especially if it has been a while.

C is wrong outright - a secretagogue does nothing in T1DM, where there are no functioning beta cells to stimulate.

stem: Having addressed the sources of variability, which escalation does the facilitator identify as preferred for all individuals with type 1 diabetes? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)
answer:
The correct answer is C, an insulin pump - stated in the deck as preferred for all individuals with T1DM.

The full escalation pathway: address variability → DEC → full basal-bolus MDI, with rapid-acting insulin before breakfast, lunch and supper dosed on a correction factor plus carbohydrate intake, and a longer-acting basal (glargine, degludec) instead of Levemir/detemir → CGM, subject to coverage → insulin pump.

stem: A family doctor calls you at 4:30 pm on the Friday before the May long weekend about Fitzwilliam Darcy, a 55-year-old man with a random plasma glucose of 55 mmol/L. He has no history of diabetes but has had two weeks of increased thirst, blurred vision and polyuria every half hour. Which type of diabetes is most likely? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Type 1 diabetes, because of the severity of the hyperglycemia
Type 2 diabetes, which is also the most common form of diabetes overall

answer: The correct answer is B. Type 2 diabetes is most likely and it is the most common form of diabetes overall. Severity of hyperglycemia alone does not classify the diabetes - a glucose of 55 mmol/L is entirely compatible with T2DM presenting as HHS.

lecture: DSSG Case 3 - Fitzwilliam Darcy (Random Plasma Glucose 55 mmol/L)
lectureMeta: Source: Week 2 DSSG "Diabetes Mellitus Cases", facilitator deck by Mohammed Alagha. Q30-38. Tests [[06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes]] and [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: You ask the family doctor for the serum creatinine, electrolytes including sodium and bicarbonate with an anion gap, and Mr. Darcy's mental status. What are you screening for? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)
answer:
The correct answer is A. Both are potentially lethal and both need to be excluded before anything is deferred over a long weekend.

  • HHS - suggested by impaired mental status plus an effective serum osmolality ≥ ~320 mosm/kg.
  • DKA - suggested by an anion-gap metabolic acidosis, which is why the bicarbonate and anion gap were requested.

lecture: DSSG Case 3 - Fitzwilliam Darcy (Random Plasma Glucose 55 mmol/L)
lectureMeta: Source: Week 2 DSSG "Diabetes Mellitus Cases", facilitator deck by Mohammed Alagha. Q30-38. Tests [[06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes]] and [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: How is the effective serum osmolality calculated in this context? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)
answer:
The correct answer is A. Effective serum osmolality = (2 × [Na⁺]) + [glucose], and a value ≥ ~320 mosm/kg together with impaired mental status is the concern for HHS.

Urea is excluded because it crosses cell membranes freely and so is not an effective osmole - it does not drive the water shift that produces the neurological findings.

stem: What advice should you give the family doctor at 4:30 pm on the Friday of a long weekend? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Send him to the Emergency Department now
Book him into your clinic on Tuesday and start metformin in the meantime
Advise oral rehydration with fruit juice and review after the weekend
Arrange outpatient labs for the following week

answer:
The correct answer is A. If he has not had the tests needed to rule out HHS and DKA, or he has had them and the results are consistent with either, the safe thing is the Emergency Department now. Both are potentially lethal if not treated quickly, so leaving it over the long weekend is not a good idea.

He should also stop drinking anything except water and diet juices - which is why C is actively harmful.

stem: Why is insulin the drug of choice for Mr. Darcy's severe new hyperglycemia, even though he most likely has type 2 diabetes? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: It is the only agent licensed in new-onset diabetes
It is the most effective option for quickly controlling severe uncontrolled hyperglycemia, and he may not need it long term
All oral agents are contraindicated in type 2 diabetes at diagnosis
It is the only agent that does not require renal dosing

answer: The correct answer is B. Because there is concern about acute decompensation, the threshold to start insulin ahead of all other anti-hyperglycemic drugs is very low. It is the most effective option for quickly controlling severe uncontrolled hyperglycemia. He may not need insulin long term - the choice is driven by the acuity, not by the eventual classification.

stem: At the Diabetes Education Centre, Mr. Darcy is seen by a nurse and a dietician. Which best describes what the nurse will cover? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Survival skills - safe insulin use, hypoglycemia, glucose monitoring, driving guidelines and sick-day management
A calorie-reduced, nutritionally balanced diet plan and carbohydrate teaching
Titration of his statin and antihypertensives

answer:
The correct answer is A. The nurse concentrates on survival skills:

  • safe use of insulin - dose setting, how to inject, injection timing, storage
  • hypoglycemia - detection, prevention, treatment
  • glucose monitoring
  • driving guidelines
  • sick-day management

B is the dietician's role - assess his current diet, then build a plan on the Diabetes Canada 2018 guidelines: nutritionally balanced and, if he is overweight, calorie-reduced for weight loss. He also learns about carbohydrates generally, and may later be taught carbohydrate counting, especially if he ends up on MDI.

stem: Mr. Darcy's father died in his early 60s of kidney failure after a leg amputation. Which statement about protecting his kidneys is correct? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Use an ACE inhibitor or an ARB, but never both together
Use an ACE inhibitor and an ARB together for additive renal protection
Neither class has a role once diabetes is diagnosed
An ARB is only indicated once dialysis has begun

answer:
The correct answer is A. For prevention of renal failure: screening urine ACR annually, blood glucose control, blood pressure control, and an ACE inhibitor or an ARB - but not both.

Dual RAAS blockade adds hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury without an offsetting benefit, which is why the "or" in that sentence is the examinable part.

stem: Is ASA used for primary or secondary cardiovascular prevention in diabetes? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Primary prevention in all patients with diabetes over 40
Neither - ASA has no role in diabetes

answer:
The correct answer is B, secondary prevention only. Meta-analyses and RCTs show that in primary prevention the benefit does not clearly exceed the harm, so ASA is not used for that indication in diabetes.

The rest of the macrovascular prevention package for coronary heart disease, ischemic stroke and peripheral vascular disease: blood pressure control, LDL-C control with a statin, smoking cessation, and anti-hyperglycemic drugs proven to prevent MACE in the cardiovascular outcome trials.

stem: Which set of interventions is used to prevent vision loss from diabetic eye disease? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Annual screening eye exam, blood glucose control, blood pressure control, smoking cessation, and fenofibrate
Laser photocoagulation for every patient at diagnosis

answer:
The correct answer is A. For diabetic eye disease: a screening eye exam roughly annually, blood glucose control, blood pressure control, smoking cessation, and fenofibrate.

Set against the other structural complications from the same slide:

  • Renal failure - screening urine ACR annually, BG control, BP control, an ACE inhibitor or an ARB.
  • Peripheral sensory neuropathy - BG control.
  • Foot ulcers / amputation - everything that prevents neuropathy and peripheral vascular disease, plus regular foot exams and patient education, especially in high-risk feet.

stem: Agnes Wickfield is a 32-year-old Air Canada pilot with polyuria and polydipsia. She is not pregnant, her random blood glucose is 25.4 mmol/L, and urinalysis shows 3+ glucosuria but is negative for ketones. Which pairing of clinical features with the diabetes type they favour is correct? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: acanthosis favours type 1; DKA at presentation favours type 2
DKA at presentation favours type 1; acanthosis favours type 2
Both DKA and acanthosis favour type 1
Neither feature has any discriminating value

answer:
The correct answer is B. DKA at presentation favours T1D; acanthosis favours T2D.

The other features available from history and exam: ethnicity (T2D more common in First Nations, African American, Asian and Hispanic populations), family history (stronger in T2D - identical-twin concordance ~100%, and ≥half of T2D patients have a close relative with diabetes, versus only ~15% of new-onset T1D having a first- or second-degree relative with T1D), past GDM (favours T2D), older age (favours T2D), and obesity (favours T2D).

flags.title: No single factor is decisive
flags.html: T1D has been described in patients in their 80s, being overweight does not protect against immune-mediated beta-cell loss, and DKA can occur in T2D. The features are combined, not applied individually.

stem: Which investigations would specifically support a diagnosis of type 1 diabetes in Agnes? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Pancreatic autoantibodies and a low serum C-peptide
A high serum C-peptide and a fasting insulin level
An OGTT and a fructosamine level

answer:
The correct answer is A.

  • Pancreatic autoantibodies - GADA, IAA, ZnT8A, IA-2A, ICA - marking immune-mediated beta-cell loss.
  • A low serum C-peptide - favours T1D, because C-peptide is co-secreted with endogenous insulin and so falls as beta-cell function is lost.
  • HLA typing - T1D is associated with DR3, DR4, DQ8.

stem: Why does it matter whether Agnes has type 1 or type 2 diabetes? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Only because the long-term complication risk differs
If she has type 1, insulin is the required treatment - and as a commercial pilot this carries direct occupational and regulatory implications
It does not change management at this glucose level
Only because type 1 requires a different A1c target

answer:
The correct answer is B. Two reasons are given:

  • If she has type 1 diabetes, insulin is the required treatment - not an option among others.
  • She is a commercial pilot, so the diagnosis and the need for insulin carry direct occupational and regulatory implications.

stem:
Patient 5 is a 22-year-old man with type 1 diabetes and an A1c of 8.4%, on rapid-acting NovoRapid before each meal and glargine 16 units at bedtime. His week of readings (mmol/L):

DayBreakfastLunchSupperBedtime
Mon4.26.812.316.7
Tue3.912.514.618.2
Wed6.88.59.212.6
Thu3.26.98.54.7
Fri4.15.211.916.5
Sat2.811.413.48.4
Sun3.99.414.315.9

Which description of his pattern is correct? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Morning hypoglycemia, with hyperglycemia at supper and at bedtime
Morning hyperglycemia, with hypoglycemia at supper and at bedtime

answer:
The correct answer is A. Reading down the columns: the breakfast values run low (2.8, 3.2, 3.9, 3.9, 4.1) - morning hypoglycemia; the supper values run high (up to 14.6) - hyperglycemia at supper; and the bedtime values run high (up to 18.2) - hyperglycemia at bedtime.

Reading the record by time of day rather than by day is the whole technique here - the pattern is in the columns, not the rows.

stem: Which set of insulin adjustments does the facilitator recommend for Patient 5? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Decrease bedtime glargine by 10-20%; increase lunch NovoRapid by 10%; increase supper NovoRapid by 10%
Increase bedtime glargine by 10-20%; decrease lunch and supper NovoRapid
Make no change and repeat the A1c in three months

answer:
The correct answer is A.

  • Decrease bedtime Lantus/glargine by 10-20% - it is the insulin acting overnight, and he is waking low.
  • Increase lunch NovoRapid by 10% - it covers the interval ending at the pre-supper reading, which is high.
  • Increase supper NovoRapid by 10% - it covers the interval ending at bedtime, which is high.

stem: What is the general principle for adjusting a basal-bolus regimen from a glucose record? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Adjust the insulin acting before the abnormal glucose, typically by 10-20%
Adjust the insulin given after the abnormal glucose
Adjust the basal insulin only, whatever the pattern
Change all components simultaneously to reach target faster

answer:
The correct answer is A. Adjust the insulin acting before the abnormal glucose, typically by 10-20%:

  • morning low → decrease the bedtime basal
  • high pre-supper → increase the lunch rapid-acting
  • high bedtime → increase the supper rapid-acting

The reading tells you which insulin was responsible for the interval that just ended.

stem: Patient 6 is a 55-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and a seizure disorder. Her A1c is 6.9%, and her record shows many single-digit readings with occasional highs. What is the concern, and what should be done? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Her control is too tight given her seizure disorder - reduce the degludec by 10-20% and consider a higher A1c target such as 7.5%
Her control is too loose - increase the degludec by 20%
Her A1c is ideal - make no change
Stop insulin entirely and start a sulfonylurea

answer:
The correct answer is A. An A1c of 6.9% is probably too tight given her seizure disorder - hypoglycemia can provoke seizures, and she is already running lots of single-digit values. The occasional high readings are likely corrections or over-corrections of a previous low, not true loss of control.

  • Reduce the Tresiba/degludec by 10-20%.
  • Consider a higher A1c target (e.g. 7.5%), especially if she has no glycemic-responsive (eye, kidney, nerve) complications.

The deck qualifies this by whether her seizures are controlled and whether she has eye, renal or neuropathic complications.

stem: Patient 7 is an 81-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, advanced dementia, living in a nursing home with caregiver-administered insulin. His A1c is 9.1% and most readings sit above the 4.0-7.0 mmol/L ac-meal target. What insulin adjustment is recommended? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Add rapid-acting insulin at every meal

answer:
The correct answer is C, none. His glucoses are high relative to the ac-meal targets needed to reach an A1c of ~7.0% - but given his dementia, older age and limited life expectancy, the glycemic goals of care shift away from preventing structural complications through a lower A1c and toward keeping him free of symptomatic hypo- and hyperglycemia.

This is the case that makes the point: the right answer to "would you change the regimen?" is sometimes no, and tightening control here would buy complication prevention he will not live to benefit from at the cost of hypoglycemia he cannot reliably report.

stem: What determines the glycemic target in an older adult? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)
answer:
The correct answer is B, functional status and life expectancy - not age. As frailty increases, targets loosen to reduce hypoglycemia risk.

StatusA1c targetIdea
Functionally independent≤7.0%treat like a younger adult
Functionally dependent<8.0%some relaxation of target
Frail / dementia<8.5%prioritise avoiding hypoglycemia
End of lifeno A1c targetavoid symptomatic hyper- and any hypoglycemia

The exact numbers are not the point - the concept is that the frailer or more dependent the patient, the looser the target, because the harm of hypoglycemia starts to outweigh the benefit of tight control. This is exactly why no adjustment was recommended for Patient 7.
